The Thirty Years' War. From 1618 to 1648, this devastating conflict ravaged Central Europe, beginning as a religious struggle between Catholic and Protestant powers within the Holy Roman Empire and escalating into a pan-European war of dynastic ambition. The war began in 1618 when Protestant nobles in Bohemia rebelled against Hapsburg Catholic rule, triggering wider religious conflict across the Holy Roman Empire. The conflict evolved into a dynastic power struggle as France, under Cardinal Richelieu and Louis XIII, intervened to break Hapsburg dominance in Europe. Sweden entered the war militarily under King Gustavus Adolphus to defend Protestant interests and gain Swedish territory and influence. Mercenary armies devastated the German territories. Entire regions were depopulated by military campaigns, famine, and disease outbreaks accompanying armies. Germany fragmented into hundreds of semi-independent principalities by war's end, and the Holy Roman Empire never recovered its former authority. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 established principles of national sovereignty and religious toleration, marking the end of religiously-motivated wars in Europe. France emerged as the war's clear winner, absorbing Alsace, gaining prestige, and displacing Spain and Austria as Europe's dominant power. Starting with a rebellion in Bohemia, the war pulled in Sweden, France, and most German territories into a grueling contest that killed roughly one-third of the German population and reshaped the political map of Europe. The Peace of Westphalia that concluded it ended both religious war in Christendom and Habsburg dominance, establishing France as Europe's paramount power.
